(healthline.com/nutrition/vegetarian-vs-vegan-vs-pescatarian), and 'Beginner's Guide to the Mediterranean Diet' (healthline.com/nutrition/mediterranean-diet-meal-plan).

1) Classic/whole-food pescatarian diet: Excludes all red meat and poultry but includes fish/seafood plus a largely plant-based intake (whole grains, legumes, nuts, seeds, fruits, vegetables, healthy fats); many also eat dairy and eggs. Healthline notes it may lower disease risk: pescatarian women gained ~2.5 fewer pounds/year than meat eaters; diabetes risk 4.8% vs 7.6% for omnivores; and ~22% lower risk of dying from heart disease. Fish supplies omega-3s (EPA/DHA), lean protein, vitamin B12, zinc and selenium. Drawbacks are limited (mainly mercury/toxins in large fish: avoid tilefish, swordfish, shark, king mackerel; limit albacore/yellowfin tuna).

2) Mediterranean (pescatarian-style) diet: Based on traditional foods of countries bordering the Mediterranean; high in plant foods, whole grains, legumes, nuts and heart-healthy fats (extra-virgin olive oil), low in animal products/meat, and includes fish/seafood at least twice a week, with poultry, eggs and dairy in moderation but red meat, processed foods, refined grains and added sugars limited. It needs no calorie counting and may help prevent weight gain, stabilize blood sugar, support heart and brain health, and reduce inflammation; it is more flexible and easier to stick to.

Comparison/conclusion: Both are seafood-and-plant-forward patterns far healthier than a typical Western diet, so both fit 'eating healthier.' The strict pescatarian diet is the more restrictive one (no poultry/red meat at all) and maximizes fish-derived omega-3s; the Mediterranean version is more flexible (allows some poultry and emphasizes olive oil) and has the strongest evidence base for heart and metabolic health. Healthline cautions that a pescatarian label alone doesn't guarantee health: it can be built on processed starches, junk food and fried fish, which is less healthy than a whole-food-based version. So for eating healthier, the best choice is a whole-food, olive-oil-rich Mediterranean-style pescatarian diet with varied fish/seafood eaten baked, grilled or sauteed rather than deep-fried.

STANDARD PESCATARIAN — excludes red meat/poultry but includes fish/seafood, dairy, eggs, and a largely plant-based base (whole grains, legumes, nuts, produce, healthy fats) with seafood as the main protein. Health benefits: lower obesity/chronic-disease risk, lower type 2 diabetes risk (4.8% vs 7.6% in omnivores), ~22% lower risk of dying from heart disease, and key omega-3 EPA/DHA for heart, brain and mood, plus protein, vitamin B12, iodine, vitamin D, zinc and selenium; flexible and easy to follow. Drawbacks: mercury/toxins in large fish (avoid tilefish, swordfish, shark, king mackerel; limit albacore/yellowfin tuna), and it can be unhealthy if based on processed starches, junk food and fish sticks. KETOTARIAN — a mostly-vegetarian keto plan allowing only eggs, fish, shellfish and ghee (all optional); <5% of calories from carbs (~25 g net), 70-75% fat, 20-25% protein; avoids meat, most dairy, soy/tofu, seed oils and nightshades. Benefits: very effective weight loss (preserves metabolic rate and lean mass, reduces hunger), blood-sugar control/type 2 diabetes, strongly anti-inflammatory, heart and brain/nervous-system benefits, gut health, nutrient-dense. Drawbacks: highly restrictive and hard to sustain long term, expensive, limited dining out, unsuitable with a history of eating disorders, and little direct research (benefits inferred from keto + vegetarian studies). VERDICT for eating healthier: Healthline's evidence favors the flexible, whole-food standard pescatarian diet as the healthier and more sustainable everyday option; the ketotarian diet is much more restrictive and mainly useful for specific goals like rapid weight loss or blood-sugar control.
